fallbackFor: Grok 4.6 timed out on the first planning phase; the owner authorized Opus 5 OAuth whenever Grok has an issue
summary: Opus 5 OAuth fallback adversarial planning audit (user-authorized fallback because Grok 4.6 timed out; this is NOT Grok evidence and carries no approval authority). Reviewed the two target documents as supplied bytes against ADR 0001, the local API threat model, and the authority manifest. Both targets are correctly framed as proposed planning evidence: ADR 0002 keeps the loopback modular monolith as the executable baseline, the threat model explicitly disclaims implementing its controls, and the authority manifest records both as `proposed` with `implementationAuthorized: false`. The topology does not silently supersede ADR 0001, and no control is claimed as shipped. However the packet is not yet safe to accept. One P0: ADR 0002 Zone 1 carves out a sanctioned "disposable, out-of-tree experiment" for a runtime that can display remote content, with no safety envelope, in a domain the authority manifest classifies as `rejected` behind EB-001; the ADR's non-authorization clause covers "desktop retention" but not this non-retained carve-out, so acceptance would grant hostile-remote-content execution authority ahead of the EB gate. Nine P1 findings follow: the EB blocker is narrowed to "retained ... that can display remote content" and contradicts migration step 7 and the manifest; the client review browser is a distinct trust zone with no data/command/secret/failure/non-owner definition despite decision driver 5; no zone or authority-table row owns secret/credential custody or the signing trust root for the receipts on which every lifecycle transition depends; the "separate appointment authority" has no place in the topology; the realtime draft store is excluded from the backup rule with no failure or degradation boundary; the public site visitor and appointment booker are absent from actors, assets, classification, and the deletion/export path; immutable artifacts plus append-only audit contradict TM-13's deletion-across-backups requirement with no reconciliation; no named human owns any zone, domain, or gate; and TM-05 asserts raw-response access control and 90-day expiry as present fact with no mechanism or owner. Five P2 and two P3 items follow. Verdict REVISE; no implementation, deployment, schema, provider, invitation, or appointment authorization is granted, and page IR/source, candidate, human approval, qualification, release, and appointment authority remain separate.

findings.sectionOrLines: Decision > Zone 1: agency client (paragraph beginning "A retained desktop runtime"); cross-check Acceptance and supersession
findings.issue: Zone 1 states: "A disposable, out-of-tree experiment may measure framework feasibility, but its output is a report, not retained product code." No envelope is attached: no prohibition on loading untrusted or remote content, no requirement for synthetic-only data, no isolation from the operator's real browser profiles, cookies, client files, or provider credentials, no network egress restriction, no time box, no artifact-deletion requirement, no named owner, and no separate owner authorization. The Acceptance clause withholds authorization for "implementation, vendor selection, schema changes, desktop retention, client invitations, deployment, or appointment activation" — a non-retained experiment is outside every listed exclusion, so acceptance of this ADR is the authorization. The authority manifest classifies the embedded-browser domain as `rejected` with the boundary "No retained desktop or browser work until a new plan closes EB-001 through EB-021, starting with EB-001," and TM-07 names EB-001 the first stop gate.
findings.risk: Accepting the ADR would permit an un-remediated embedded-browser or desktop shell to render attacker-controlled remote content on a workstation that also holds real client briefs, browser profiles, sessions, and provider credentials — the exact renderer-escape, preload-exposure, scheme-navigation, download-execution, debug-port, and cross-profile-cookie exposures EB-001 through EB-021 are blocking. "Output is a report" constrains retained code, not runtime blast radius, so the gate is bypassed by construction while appearing to be honored.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Delete the experiment sentence, or replace it with an explicitly gated envelope: no remote or untrusted content, synthetic fixtures only, no client data, no production or provider credentials, a dedicated throwaway OS profile or machine, no shared browser profile, default-deny egress, a stated time box, mandatory deletion of all artifacts, a named human owner, and separate written owner authorization recorded in the authority manifest — and state that EB-001 remains the first stop gate regardless.

findings.sectionOrLines: Decision > Zone 1 ("A retained desktop runtime that can display remote content remains blocked") vs Migration sequence step 7 vs docs/security/2026-08-29-program-threat-model.md TM-07 first bullet
findings.issue: Zone 1 scopes the EB blocker to a retained desktop runtime "that can display remote content." Migration step 7 states a broader gate ("a retained desktop package only after the desktop/browser security gate and Apple-silicon install, update, downgrade, and rollback tests pass"), and the authority manifest states "No retained desktop or browser work." TM-07 repeats the narrow phrasing ("no retained desktop or remote-content shell"). The narrowest reading permits a retained desktop shell that renders only first-party product UI without closing EB findings, even though a large share of the EB surface — packaging, signing and notarization, update and downgrade metadata, preload and IPC schema exposure, download quarantine, permission grants, public debug ports, screen-capture leakage — applies to any desktop shell regardless of whether it displays remote content.
findings.risk: Authority confusion between three documents on which desktop work is blocked. A future plan can cite Zone 1's narrow clause to retain a desktop shell while EB-001 through EB-021 remain open, defeating the stop gate and the manifest's `rejected` classification.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Restate Zone 1 and TM-07 in the manifest's terms: no retained desktop or embedded-browser product code of any kind — remote-content-capable or not — until a rewritten plan maps every EB-001 through EB-021 finding to an owner, oracle, and exit gate, and the desktop security and Apple-silicon install/update/downgrade/rollback gates in migration step 7 pass.

findings.sectionOrLines: Decision ("five deployable trust zones") and topology diagram node "Client review browser"; Zones 1–5
findings.issue: The diagram names "Client review browser" as a top-level participant and decision driver 5 requires that "Client review must be less privileged than agency authoring," but no zone section defines it. Zone 1 covers only the agency client. The least-trusted human surface therefore has no stated data boundary (what candidate bytes, evidence, assets, comments, and other tenants' data it may hold or cache), no command boundary (which commands a guest principal may issue), no secret boundary (guest link/session custody, whether an invitation token is bearer-only, forwarding and expiry), no failure boundary (behavior on expired invitation, revoked membership, superseded candidate), and no non-owner list.
findings.risk: An undefined trust zone is later specified by whichever implementation plan reaches it first. Guest scope, invitation minting, candidate-lock interaction, revocation, and stale approval — the exact set TM-06 says must pass before E6 — have no architectural anchor, so client review can drift toward agency-equivalent privilege.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a Zone 1b (or Zone 6) "client review surface" section with the same five boundary statements used for Zones 2–5, explicitly listing non-owners (membership, invitation minting, candidate lock, qualification, release, deployment credentials, other candidates and projects) and binding it to the P3 review-origin threat model that TM-06 requires.

findings.sectionOrLines: Authority and data ownership table; Zone 3 ("a signed or integrity-bound receipt"); Zone 5 ("Provider credentials are isolated to the adapter's project and environment scope")
findings.issue: The authority table has no row for secrets or credential custody, and no zone is named the owner of secret storage, issuance, rotation, or revocation. Zone 2 states only what it is not ("does not serve as a general browser credential store"). Zone 3 requires each job to return "a signed or integrity-bound receipt" and Zone 3/Zone 5 make the control plane advance lifecycle state only "after validating the receipt," but no document names the signing key custodian, the verification trust root, key rotation, compromise revocation, or what happens to receipts already signed under a compromised key. Neither document contains a threat domain for key management, secret rotation, or post-compromise recovery; TM-13 covers support access and offboarding only.
findings.risk: Receipts are the linchpin of the entire authority chain from gate to qualification to release. With no custody owner and no trust root, a later design can place signing material inside the job plane, the realtime plane, or a shared control-plane store, letting a compromised worker or media service forge a qualification or release receipt — a cross-boundary authority escalation the ADR's driver 7 explicitly forbids. Absent rotation and revocation, a single key leak has no defined containment path.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add an authority-table row for "Secrets, signing keys, and provider credentials" naming a single custody owner and explicit non-owners (model, skill, worker, realtime/media plane, agency client, client review browser, generated site), and add a threat domain (or extend TM-09/TM-10) covering key issuance, rotation, compromise revocation, receipt re-verification after key rotation, and post-compromise recovery, each with an oracle.

findings.sectionOrLines: Decision topology diagram; Zones 1–5; Authority and data ownership table row "Appointment state"
findings.issue: The table asserts "Appointment state | Separate appointment authority and release identity | Website rollback or re-delivery," and TM-12 requires separate appointment candidate, approval, activation, revocation, and release IDs. But the topology defines no location for that separate authority: it is absent from the diagram and from all five zones. It is not stated whether the appointment authority is a distinct deployable, a bounded context inside the Zone 2 control plane, a separate runtime adapter behind the delivery origin, or a third-party service — nor who owns its data, commands, secrets, failure modes, and non-owner list.
findings.risk: "Separate authority" is asserted without a boundary that makes it separable. If it is later implemented inside the same control plane and release path by default, the TM-12 threats (website rollback restoring stale appointment configuration, revoked appointment authority returning through re-delivery, shared deployment identity conflating site and appointment release) become structurally available despite the stated separation. Placement is a topology decision affecting an existing owner-approved-architecture domain.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Either add an explicit zone/section for the appointment authority with its data, command, secret, failure, and non-owner boundaries and place it in the diagram, or state plainly that appointment topology placement is deferred to a separate ADR and is out of scope for ADR 0002 — and record that deferral in the authority manifest's appointment-acquisition boundary.

findings.sectionOrLines: Consistency and failure rules ("Backups protect control-plane metadata and immutable artifacts"); Zone 4; Authority table row "Draft comments and presence"
findings.issue: The backup rule is scoped to control-plane metadata and immutable artifacts. The realtime draft store — which the authority table makes the owner of draft comments and presence, and which Zone 4 lets CRDTs use for draft text — is excluded, with no stated durability, backup, retention, or restore expectation and no recorded acceptance of loss. Zone 4 also has no failure boundary: nothing states whether authoring, review, or comment capture degrades safely, blocks, or silently drops data when the realtime plane is unavailable or partitioned, nor how draft state that never reached the control plane is recovered.
findings.risk: Client review comments and unaccepted draft text — the inputs to named-human decisions — can be permanently lost with no owner, no oracle, and no accepted risk record. A silent realtime outage could also cause reviewers to believe comments were captured when they were not, producing approvals against an incomplete review record.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: State the realtime draft store's durability and backup class explicitly (backed up, or ephemeral with a named accepted-loss owner and a client-visible unsaved/degraded indicator), and add a Zone 4 failure rule: realtime unavailability degrades to a visible read-only or offline state and never silently discards or implicitly accepts draft content; add a corresponding TM-06 oracle.

findings.sectionOrLines: Actors; Assets and security properties; Data classification and model/export policy; TM-11; TM-12; TM-13
findings.issue: The public site visitor, form submitter, and appointment booker — end users of the client's client — appear nowhere as actors, nowhere in the assets table, and nowhere in the data-classification table. Assets lists "Appointment records" with a lifecycle property only, never a confidentiality or retention property. TM-11 covers form spam, destinations, and consent behavior but not the personal data those forms and bookings collect. TM-13's deletion and export controls are tenant- and client-offboarding-scoped ("incomplete tenant deletion," "client offboarding revokes sessions..."); there is no path for an individual data subject's access, correction, deletion, or objection, and no retention tier for submission or booking data.
findings.risk: The largest population of personal data in the shipped product — end-user names, contact details, message bodies, and appointment times captured by generated public sites — has no classification, no retention default, no deletion path, no telemetry rule, and no external-model rule. This is a credible privacy and regulatory exposure and it is invisible to every oracle in the document, so no phase gate would catch it.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add "public end user / form submitter / appointment booker" to Actors; add "public submission and appointment personal data" to the assets table with confidentiality, purpose limitation, and retention properties; give it an explicit row in the data-classification table (external model/audit, telemetry, default retention); and extend TM-13's controls and oracles to individual data-subject access, deletion, and export in addition to tenant deletion.

findings.sectionOrLines: Assets and security properties ("Candidate artifacts and receipts: Immutable identity..."; "Audit log: Append-only semantics"); TM-03 controls; TM-13 controls and oracles ("deletion across primary/queue/cache/backup"); ADR 0002 Consistency and failure rules
findings.issue: Two required properties in the same document are in direct tension with no stated reconciliation. TM-03 requires every mutation to produce a new immutable candidate whose exact hashes bind every gate and decision, and the assets table requires immutable candidate artifacts and an append-only audit log; TM-13 simultaneously requires complete tenant deletion across primary, queue, cache, and backup, plus deletion receipts and encrypted backups with "tenant-aware restore and deletion handling." No mechanism reconciles them (for example crypto-shredding with per-tenant keys, redaction-in-place with integrity-preserving tombstones, or a documented, owner-accepted carve-out for audit evidence under legal hold). ADR 0002's backup rule likewise requires restore drills to prove referential integrity between candidate, decision, and release IDs, which deletion of candidate bytes would break.
findings.risk: Whichever requirement is implemented first silently defeats the other: either deletion is incomplete (a privacy and offboarding failure the document itself calls a threat), or artifacts and audit entries are hard-deleted and the release-integrity, rollback, and non-repudiation chain becomes unverifiable — with restore drills then failing referential integrity. The contradiction is currently unownable because no oracle tests both properties together.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add an explicit reconciliation statement naming the mechanism (for example per-tenant key destruction rendering artifacts unreadable while identities, hashes, and receipts survive) and the exact audit evidence preserved after deletion, plus a combined oracle: delete a tenant, then run the restore drill and prove both that content is unrecoverable and that candidate/decision/release referential integrity still holds.

findings.sectionOrLines: ADR: Status line, Zone 5 ("Named release owner"), Acceptance and supersession; threat model: Risk acceptance and closure, Review and maintenance, TM-11 ("explicit per-capability runtime owner")
findings.issue: Both documents make named-human ownership the closure condition — "a named release owner," "explicit per-capability runtime owner," "Risk acceptance must name the risk, scope, expiry, compensating control, owner, and evidence," "A phase is ready only when every applicable threat has an owner, oracle, implementation ticket," "Each review records the exact document hash, changed threat IDs, owner, and linked tickets" — yet neither document names a single human for any zone, any of the thirteen threat domains, any P0 gate, the EB remediation, the threat-model review itself, or the ADR acceptance. The ADR's owner is referenced only as "the owner" and "owner acceptance required."
findings.risk: Every gate in the packet is unassignable as written. No accountable person can be shown to have accepted a risk, closed a finding, or authorized a release, which is precisely the condition that lets model output, audit prose, or default behavior fill an authority vacuum. It also makes the packet's own readiness criterion unsatisfiable at review time.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add an owner column or table assigning a named human (or a named role bound to a specific person in the authority manifest) to each of Zones 1–5, each TM-01 through TM-13 domain, the EB-001–EB-021 remediation, and threat-model review, and name the accepting owner on the ADR status line.

findings.sectionOrLines: Data classification and model/export policy, final paragraph ("Raw Grok audit packets exclude... raw responses are access-controlled and expire after 90 days...")
findings.issue: This paragraph is written in the present indicative as a statement of current fact, unlike the rest of the document, which the Purpose section explicitly frames as required future controls ("It does not claim the current code implements these controls"). No access-control mechanism, storage location, custodian, expiry job, or deletion receipt is named, and the packet supplies no evidence that either the exclusion or the 90-day expiry is enforced. The audit artifacts referenced by the authority manifest live under a version-controlled `docs/audits/` tree; once such files are committed, a time-based expiry is not achievable by deletion alone, and no history-rewrite or alternate-store policy is stated.
findings.risk: A retention and access-control commitment asserted as implemented, in the very document that defines the data-classification policy, invites downstream documents and reviewers to treat it as satisfied. If raw model responses in fact persist indefinitely in version control, the stated Confidential/Restricted handling rules are contradicted by the storage medium and there is no owner to detect it.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Rewrite the paragraph in the same required-future-control voice as the rest of the document, name the storage location and custodian, state whether raw responses may be committed to version control at all, and add an oracle (audit-artifact census plus expiry check). If they are already committed, record that as an accepted exception with owner, scope, and expiry rather than as a satisfied control.

findings.sectionOrLines: Header "Related: ADR 0002, local API threat model, embedded-browser audit EB-001–EB-021"; TM-07 first bullet; ADR 0002 Zone 1
findings.issue: Both documents make EB-001 through EB-021 a blocking gate but neither cites a path or document hash for the findings register, and the only location the supplied manifest associates with those IDs is `docs/audits/grok-4.6/2026-08-29-embedded-browser-plan-audit.md`. The manifest sets `forbiddenPrimaryPathPrefixes: ["docs/audits/"]` and states that audit artifacts cannot authorize implementation, so the contents of a blocking gate are defined only inside a class of artifact the governance model forbids as a primary authority — and the twenty-one findings are not enumerated, owned, or hashed anywhere in the packet.
findings.risk: The gate cannot be verified closed or open against exact bytes, and the count or numbering could drift (findings merged, renumbered, or silently narrowed) without detection. A blocking condition whose content lives only in a non-authoritative path is weakly enforceable.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Create or cite a non-audit-path findings register (for example under `docs/security/` or a tickets manifest) that enumerates EB-001 through EB-021 with title, owner, oracle, exit gate, and current open state, and reference it from both documents by path and document hash.

findings.sectionOrLines: Status/Supersedes header lines; Migration sequence steps 1 and 6; Acceptance and supersession
findings.issue: ADR 0001's "Revisit when" clause requires revisiting that ADR "before introducing a second deployable or moving run/evidence authority outside this repository." ADR 0002 proposes five deployable zones and makes the cloud control plane the system of record for run source-authority selection, but records only "Supersedes: no current runtime decision" and "Revisits after acceptance: ADR 0001 for the future hosted product only." ADR 0001 itself carries no back-link or annotation, so a reader arriving at ADR 0001 (which the manifest lists as accepted baseline and as a related path for the engineering-operating-system domain) sees no indication that a successor topology is proposed. Migration step 6 permits extracting "one deployable seam at a time" without singling out the seam that moves run/evidence authority off `sites/<id>/` as requiring its own accepted ADR, data-migration, and rollback plan.
findings.risk: The most consequential migration step — relocating run and evidence authority out of the local filesystem — is covered only by the general supersession clause and could proceed as an ordinary seam extraction, bypassing the revisit ADR 0001 requires. One-directional linkage also risks ADR 0001 being read as the whole picture.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a back-link/annotation in ADR 0001 pointing to proposed ADR 0002, state explicitly in ADR 0002 which ADR 0001 revisit triggers it does and does not discharge, and amend migration step 6 to require a separately accepted ADR plus a data-migration, dual-run, and rollback plan before run or evidence authority leaves the local per-run artifacts.

findings.sectionOrLines: Decision topology diagram ("public delivery origin"); Zones 1–5; Authority and data ownership table
findings.issue: The diagram's terminal node, the public delivery origin, has no zone section — it is the boundary facing wholly untrusted internet traffic, yet its data, command, secret, failure, and non-owner boundaries appear only indirectly through the "Public delivery" table row and TM-11. Separately, the authority table omits rows for tenant/user identity and project membership, the audit log, and billing/metering, even though all three are named as authoritative concerns in Zone 2 and in TM-01 and TM-13.
findings.risk: Boundaries that exist only implicitly get assigned by implementation convenience. Membership authority in particular is contested by the realtime/media plane and guest invitation flows, which TM-06 already identifies as an escalation path; without a table row and explicit non-owner list, the ADR's own driver 7 has no anchor for that boundary.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a short zone section for the public delivery origin with the five boundary statements, and add authority-table rows for identity and project membership, audit log, and billing/metering, each with explicit non-owners.

findings.sectionOrLines: ADR Consistency and failure rules (backup/restore bullet); threat model TM-13 controls and oracles; Data classification table "Default retention" column
findings.issue: Recovery is specified qualitatively only. There is no recovery point or recovery time objective, no drill cadence, no scenario for total loss of the immutable artifact store (on which every rollback and re-delivery depends), and no statement of what "last known-good release" means if artifacts are unavailable. Retention defaults are likewise unmeasurable: Confidential defaults to "minimum project need" and Internal to "active project plus policy window," neither of which any oracle can evaluate; the only concrete number in the packet is the 90-day figure flagged in F-10.
findings.risk: Recovery and retention cannot be tested, so the restore-drill and telemetry/export oracles cannot fail. TM-03's requirement to preserve the last known-good release and TM-10's rollback drill both depend on artifact-store survivability that is never bounded.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add RPO/RTO targets and a drill cadence, add an artifact-store-loss scenario with its effect on rollback and re-delivery, and replace the qualitative retention defaults with bounded values or a named policy document that supplies them.

findings.sectionOrLines: Actors ("attacker: ... or insider"); Assets table row "Audit log"; TM-01 controls; ADR 0002 Zone 5 ("Named release owner")
findings.issue: "Insider" is listed once in the attacker enumeration but no threat domain addresses privileged-insider abuse. The audit log requires "append-only semantics" with no WORM storage, external anchoring, independent copy, or tamper-evidence beyond the word semantics, and the same administrative principals who can change membership and policy would be able to reach it. Production release requires only a single "named release owner"; no separation of duties, two-person rule, or independent verification is required for the highest-authority action in the system, and TM-01 asks only for step-up authentication.
findings.risk: A single compromised or malicious privileged account can authorize a release and then alter or suppress the evidence of it. Since the audit log is the evidence of record for every named-human decision, its integrity against the most privileged actor determines whether any other control can be proven after the fact.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add tamper-evidence for the audit log (append-only storage plus periodic external anchoring or an independent copy outside the administrative boundary, with access logging of reads) and state whether production release and membership/credential changes require a second named approver; add an insider-abuse oracle.

findings.sectionOrLines: Zones 1–5 and Portable delivery artifact ("Release 1 produces a deterministic static Website artifact...", "The API edge authenticates a principal...")
findings.issue: The ADR body is written in the present indicative throughout, describing target behavior in the same voice used for existing behavior. Unlike the threat model, which opens with "It does not claim the current code implements these controls," the ADR's equivalent disclaimer appears only in the Context, Consequences, and Acceptance sections, far from the zone descriptions most likely to be quoted in isolation.
findings.risk: Quoted out of context, a zone paragraph reads as a description of a shipped system, which is exactly the drift the authority manifest's `proposed` class exists to prevent.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a one-line "target state; not current behavior" note at the head of the Decision section, or convert the zone and artifact descriptions to explicit target voice ("will" / "must").

findings.sectionOrLines: Threat domains TM-01 through TM-13; cross-check ADR 0002 Migration sequence step 5
findings.issue: ADR 0002 names data residency as a precondition for infrastructure selection ("Select infrastructure only after tenancy, data residency, recovery, cost, operational, and conformance evidence exists"), but no threat domain covers residency or cross-border transfer: not in TM-01 tenancy, TM-05 model routing (where provider region determines where confidential prompts land), TM-08 workers, or TM-13 backups and export. TM-06 mentions jurisdiction only for recording consent.
findings.risk: Residency is treated as a selection criterion with no threat, control, or oracle, so a compliant selection could still be defeated by a model provider region, worker placement, or backup replication decision made elsewhere.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add residency and cross-border transfer as controls and oracles under TM-05 (model routing region), TM-08 (worker placement), and TM-13 (backup replication and export destination), or state explicitly that residency is deferred to the infrastructure-selection packet.

acceptedStrengths: The current loopback monolith is not silently superseded: ADR 0002 states "The current modular monolith remains the implementation baseline," "ADR 0001 remains authoritative for the current executable system," and migration step 1 keeps the local monolith and Page IR work as the executable baseline. The threat model correspondingly states "The local API threat model remains authoritative for the executable loopback product."

No proposed control is claimed as implemented, with one exception (F-10). The threat model opens with "It does not claim the current code implements these controls," and the ADR closes with "This proposed ADR is planning evidence only... Acceptance does not authorize implementation, vendor selection, schema changes, desktop retention, client invitations, deployment, or appointment activation."

The supplied authority manifest corroborates the framing: `target-topology` and `program-security` are both `proposed` with `implementationAuthorized: false`, and `implementationAuthorized: false` holds at the program level, so neither target document currently confers authority.

Authority separation is stated crisply and repeatedly: "Model, skill, browser, and collaboration output is a proposal or event; none is release authority" (driver 3); "No model, skill, worker, provider callback, transcript, browser page, or test suite is a human approval actor"; and TM-05's requirement that models cannot receive authority-class tools.

One-source-authority-per-run is preserved and matches the manifest's website-source boundary: "`page-ir-v1` or the closed `template-v1` compatibility path, never both and never a mid-run switch," with Page IR listed as non-owned by Canvas DOM, model output, browser capture, and CRDT.

The CRDT/realtime subordination rule is correct and explicit: CRDTs own draft text and awareness only and "never merge Page IR, candidate state, approval, or release authority"; the media service cannot mint invitations, change candidate locks, approve, or deploy; E6 stays blocked behind P3's gates.

Failure semantics fail closed rather than inferring success: at-least-once delivery with durable deduplication, prior-receipt replay for exact retries, stale-result rejection, and "Queue exhaustion, worker loss, provider ambiguity, or network partition parks the transition. It does not infer success."

Release integrity is well specified: one immutable qualified candidate plus one explicit authorization, post-success verification of deployed bytes, manifest, headers, TLS, and domain ownership, callbacks as evidence only with polling reconciliation, and preservation of the prior rollbackable release through an observation window.

Vendor neutrality is held: the ADR explicitly declines to select database, identity, realtime, hosting, model, desktop, or deployment providers, and "Choose named vendors now" is a recorded rejected alternative on the grounds that vendor semantics would become product authority.

The fallback-review rule is stated correctly and matches this session's authorization: Grok 4.6 review is mandatory input but never approval, and "a different model is explicitly recorded as a user-authorized fallback, not called Grok evidence."

Appointment independence is asserted at both the authority-table level and in a dedicated TM-12 domain covering revoke-then-rollback, version skew, duplicate/timeout replay, and visible runtime downshift that never claims a booking — the correct threat set, even though its topology placement is missing (F-05).

Severity definitions and closure discipline are sound: P0/P1 block, risk acceptance must name risk, scope, expiry, compensating control, owner, and evidence, "A model cannot accept risk," and threat-model review is explicitly evidence rather than implementation authorization.
missingEvidence: No filesystem or command tooling was available in this session, so the exact aggregate SHA-256 (2f1cc311863c3f84e67bed9ba46cd8798da6dd604bbb0e683e93690f69897dc4) and the per-file hashes for docs/adr/0002-target-desktop-cloud-topology.md and docs/security/2026-08-29-program-threat-model.md could not be recomputed against repository bytes. All hashes and byte counts are accepted as supplied and were not independently verified.

The EB-001 through EB-021 findings register was not supplied. It is impossible to verify from this packet that all twenty-one findings remain open, that none were merged, renumbered, or narrowed, or that the two target documents' blocking language covers their actual content.

Neither `docs/plans/one-box-master/01-foundation/release-1-contract.md` nor the compatibility matrix was supplied, so ADR 0002 migration step 2 and the "Release 1 produces a deterministic static Website artifact" claim could not be checked against the Release 1 contract.
`docs/security/supply-chain-policy.md` was not supplied, so TM-09's controls could not be reconciled with the accepted supply-chain policy or the adoption ledger.
`docs/eval/one-box-program/evaluation-strategy.md` was not supplied, so the thirteen threat domains' oracles could not be checked for corresponding evaluation coverage.

`docs/tickets/one-box-program/manifest.json` was not supplied, so the threat model's readiness criterion ("every applicable threat has an owner, oracle, implementation ticket") could not be evaluated for any domain.
The P3 review-origin threat model referenced as E6's blocking gate (TM-06, ADR Zone 4) was not supplied and may not yet exist; its status is unverified.

No owner acceptance record was supplied for either target document beyond the manifest's `proposed` classification, and no named human is identified anywhere in the packet as accepting owner, release owner, or domain owner.
No repository, runtime, test, vendor, legal/license, or user-research evidence was supplied or generated; nothing in this review asserts current code behavior.
No evidence was supplied of any access-control or expiry mechanism for raw model-audit responses (F-10); the claim could not be confirmed or refuted.

phaseDecision.reason: One P0 and nine P1 findings. The P0 is a live authorization hazard rather than a documentation gap: ADR 0002's Zone 1 sanctions a disposable out-of-tree experiment for a runtime that can display remote content, with no safety envelope, and the ADR's non-authorization clause covers only "desktop retention" — so accepting the ADR as written would authorize hostile-remote-content execution in a domain the authority manifest classifies as rejected behind EB-001. The P1 set adds a narrowed EB blocker that contradicts migration step 7 and the manifest, an undefined client-review trust zone, no secret-custody owner or signing trust root for the receipts that gate every lifecycle transition, an appointment authority with no place in the topology, a realtime draft store outside the backup rule and with no failure boundary, a wholly missing public-end-user data subject, an unreconciled immutability-versus-deletion contradiction, no named human owner for any zone or gate, and one retention control asserted as implemented.
